'The economics project. Due tomorrow.'
'Isn't it a group of six?'

The shared pantry on the second floor has become a problem. I inspected it on Monday: a stack of unwashed pans, curry dried on the stove and a smell that reached the corridor. Ramesh said he'd stopped cooking because the kitchen was too dirty to use. So now eight students are ordering food they can barely afford, and everyone is irritated with everyone. Next step: I will meet all eight residents on Thursday to agree a cleaning rota, with names on the door.

Sunday night.
Our flat's kitchen is officially a crime scene. Four of us, one sink, and it's been piling up for a week. Tonight I wanted to make instant noodles and there was no clean pot. I stood there feeling righteous: I only left a cup and one spoon! Then I saw Naveen's pan, Kunal's plates and the rice pot nobody has touched since Wednesday. And I realised every one of us thinks 'my cup is small, it doesn't matter.' That's how you get a sink full of four people's 'small' things. Naveen walked in, saw me glaring at his pan, and said, 'Bro, your cup is in there too.' Fair. We ended up washing everything together at midnight, arguing about whose turn it was. Tomorrow I'm drawing up a rota.
Mridul

passage: I'm Yogesh, and last year our shared art studio in Baroda almost fell apart over paint. Ten of us chipped in for a common cupboard of canvases and colours, and within two months it was empty, half the tubes left open to dry. Everyone blamed everyone. Charu stopped coming. I'll admit I'd taken a whole tube of cobalt blue for a commission without saying. So at our monthly meeting I said that first. Then I proposed three things: a sign-out notebook on the cupboard door, a monthly limit per person and a rotating keeper who restocks and checks. Anyone who went over would chip in extra, and we'd review it in two months. I took the first keeper month. It felt petty at first, writing 'one tube white' in a notebook. passage:
Block development officer's note, Kodipalli village, March visit.
The common grazing land here had been overgrazed for years; every family added goats, assuming one more wouldn't matter, and by last summer it was bare. Raghav, the young ward member, has done something the older members did not. He counted the animals himself, family by family, and posted the numbers at the temple. At the gram sabha he proposed limits per household, a rotation leaving one field to rest each season, and two monitors chosen by lot, changing monthly. He moved his own family's two extra goats to his uncle's village first. Uma, from the women's group, proposed the consequence: families over the limit give labour to clear the resting field. It passed. Grass is already returning in the east field. I recommend this model for neighbouring villages.

qa.q: Where did Raghav post the animal numbers?
qa.a: At the temple.

qa.q: What does Raghav moving his family's goats first suggest about his attitude?
qa.a: It suggests Raghav felt responsible and determined to be fair, willing to follow the rule before asking others.

qa.q: Why do monitors chosen by lot matter?
qa.a: Random, changing monitors keep the checking fair and trusted, so no family feels singled out.

qa.q: How might Uma see her role in the plan?
qa.a: Uma likely feels included and valued, since her proposal for the consequence was adopted by the gram sabha.

grounding: An officer notes a young village member setting fair grazing limits, rotation and shared monitoring, and following them first.

Class 4 note, Diwali fair week.
We played the market game in maths: pairs trade coloured tokens, and if both partners trade honestly, both earn five points; if one cheats while the other is honest, the cheater earns eight and the honest one gets zero. Omkar and Sharmila were partners. In round one both traded honestly. In round two Omkar hesitated, whispered, 'What if she cheats?', and handed over a fake token. Sharmila had played fair. She got zero and cried. In round three she cheated too, and both got one point. Afterwards Omkar said, 'I only cheated because I thought she would.' We talked as a class about how fear of being cheated can make both people lose. Next week we'll replay it with partners allowed to talk first.

qa.q: What happens if one partner cheats and the other is honest?
qa.a: The cheater earns eight and the honest one gets zero.

qa.a: Omkar felt anxious and afraid of being the one cheated, which pushed him to cheat first.

qa.q: Why is letting partners talk first a good change?
qa.a: Talking lets them promise honesty and build trust, which can reduce the fear that drives cheating.

qa.q: How did Sharmila react after being cheated in round two?
qa.a: Sharmila cried and then cheated in round three, hurt and unwilling to be left with nothing again.

grounding: A teacher's festival-week note shows a boy cheating in a trading game because he feared his partner would cheat first.

passage: Elif and Layla had got the same grade in every history project at their Berlin school, so when they were paired for the presentation on the Silk Road, both relaxed. So Elif spent the week at the ice rink, and Layla binge-watched a series with her cousin. The night before, they finally texted. 'How many slides do you have?' 'I thought YOU had slides.' They stayed up until two cobbling something together. The next day Elif stumbled over dates, and Layla's slides had typos. They got a C, their worst ever. In the corridor Layla said quietly, 'If we'd each done our bit instead of counting on the other, we'd both have done better.'

passage: At the coaching centre in Kota, the chemistry teacher paired Kamal and Seema for a joint problem set worth ten marks, one grade for both.
